threatType.name: Linking
threatType.description: Learning more about an individual or a group by associating data items or user actions. Linking may lead to unwanted privacy implications, even if it does not reveal one's identity.
threatType.fullDescription:
Linking refers to any act of associating different data elements to each other (incl. metadata) in such a way that it leads to undesirable privacy implications. This means that the combination of related data items will reveal (additional) information about a data subject (or groups of data subjects). By matching several data items based on recurring attributes or properties, a user profile (or group profile) can be built. Simply put, linking means learning more about an individual (or a group) by matching related data items together. Linking typically relies on a recurring identifier, a combination of attributes (quasi-identifiers) or profile that allows data to be singled out. This means that one can be confident it all belongs to the same individual (without necessarily revealing the individual's identity). In addition, linking can also be applied to data of several individuals by matching similar properties in order to learn additional information about the group as a whole.
Many systems may require linking data items to meet functional requirements (e.g., keep track of a user's session so they do not need to provide their login credentials for every request). However, `Linking' threat analysis looks at situations in which this ability to tie things together, to learn or infer additional properties is considered problematic or undesirable.

characteristic.name: Linked data
characteristic.description: Linking through identifiers
characteristic.fullDescription: Identifiers refer to any data item that can be used to uniquely identify entries or interactions and link them to the same individual.

characteristic.name: Unique identifier
characteristic.description: Linking based on an identifier that is unique (globally or locally, within the system or across the context boundary)
characteristic.fullDescription: Unique identifiers make it trivial to link multiple data items together (whether in databases or from multiple interactions with a system) as belonging to the same individual.

characteristicExample.name: Email address as ID
characteristicExample.description: Using an email address as an identifier enables the linking of all activities to the same individual, even across multiple services.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Many services frequently rely on email addresses as IDs in their services. This makes their users easily linkable across different services on which they use the same email address.

characteristicExample.name: IP addresses
characteristicExample.description: An IP address can be used to link multiple visits to the same individual.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: IP addresses are unique to a particular device. This makes it possible to link traffic from that IP to the same device and to the user of that device.

characteristicExample.name: Logged in web shop
characteristicExample.description: All product views in a web shop are linked to the same user because they are logged in.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: When a user is logged into an online service, all traffic in the context of that login session can be linked to that user. In the case of a web shop, this allows the organization to link all items viewed to that user to determine their product preferences.

characteristicExample.name: User IDs
characteristicExample.description: User IDs can be used to link different requests to the same user.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: User IDs are less directly linked to an individual as they are not as unique as an email address. However, users can reuse their user IDs across multiple services which enables linking the activity of those users across these services.

impact.name: Construct profile
impact.description: Unique identifiers facilitate the linking of new data items to a user profile, accumulating growing amounts of personal data associated with this profile. This can later lead to `Identifying' threats.

criteria.name: Unique identifier
criteria.description: Is there an identifier (unique in system/session) or dataset?

criteria.name: Linked data (what is linked?)
criteria.description: Is there other data associated with that identifier?
criteria.fullDescription: Which other data is associated with that identifier (e.g., because they are sent together)?

criteria.name: Linked data (what is it linked to?)
criteria.description: Is there previous data with the same identifier to which new data can be linked?
criteria.fullDescription: Is there other data with the same identifier to which the new data can be linked?

additionalInformation.name: Authenticated users
additionalInformation.description: Linking is especially easy for authenticated users, as all requests in the same session are linked.
additionalInformation.fullDescription: Authentication is a very common use case in which all requests are linked to the same user to prevent them from having to provide their credentials for every request. This, of course, makes all that activity also linkable to that individual. Consider to which extent authentication is required, and whether other solutions such as proving particular attributes (for example, the user only proves to be an employee at company X rather than providing all account details) would be sufficient to determine access control decisions.

characteristic.name: Linkable data
characteristic.description: Linking through the combination or analysis of data
characteristic.fullDescription: Data can be linked through the combination of threat types or datasets, or the application of more advanced profiling techniques.

characteristic.name: Through Combination
characteristic.description: Linking through combination
characteristic.fullDescription: Linking through combination involves linking by combining different data items or actions together. The items are not linked through an explicit identifier.

characteristic.name: Quasi-identifier combining data of a single individual
characteristic.description: Linking through a set of attributes that can serve as a quasi-identifier
characteristic.fullDescription: Even if there are no identifiers in the considered data, it is possible that a combined set of items is unique and can be used for linking the data.

characteristicExample.name: Location trace
characteristicExample.description: A small set of locations can be used to uniquely link activity to a single user.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Location traces are highly unique to individuals. Four spatio-temporal points are enough to uniquely link 95 percent of individuals.

characteristicExample.name: Age-gender-postalcode
characteristicExample.description: A subset of attributes may be sufficient to uniquely link data to a particular individual.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: While there may not be a single attribute or identifier in the data set, a combination of attributes may be enough to uniquely link items to a particular individual.

characteristicExample.name: Browser fingerprint
characteristicExample.description: A browser fingerprint combines properties (OS, browser, display size, ...) that together are unique to a website visitor.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: A browser fingerprint represents a combination of web client properties (operating system, browser, version, display size, ...) that together allows tracking a unique website visitor even without that visitor logging in or their browser sending cookies.

characteristicExample.name: Fine-grained raw data
characteristicExample.description: Fine-grained raw data is stored that enables linking specific entries to individuals.

impact.name: Construct profile
impact.description: The use of quasi-identifiers enables the linking of new data items to a user profile to gather increasing amounts of personal data, even without unique identifiers.
impact.fullDescription: The use of quasi-identifiers enables the linking of new data items to a user profile to gather increasing amounts of personal data linked to this profile. Even when no unique identifiers are present in the data, this can later lead to `Identifying' threats.

criteria.name: Quasi-identifier
criteria.description: Is there a set of attributes that can serve as an identifier?
criteria.fullDescription: Instead of a single identifier, is there a set of attributes that can serve as an identifier to distinguish between different data subjects?

criteria.name: Linked data (what is linked)
criteria.description: Is there other data sent together with that quasi-identifier?

criteria.name: Linked data (to which linked)
criteria.description: Is there existing data to link it to?
criteria.fullDescription: Is there data with that quasi-identifier to which the new data can be linked?

additionalInformation.name: Combined properties
additionalInformation.description: Many requests contain a lot of different properties that, when combined, are unique to an individual.

characteristic.name: Combining data of different individuals
characteristic.description: Linking through combining data
characteristic.fullDescription: By joining datasets or records of different individuals, additional information can be inferred about these individuals.

characteristicExample.name: Social network indirect relations
characteristicExample.description: Relations in a social network indirectly contain information about individuals not on that social network.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Individuals that are not a member of the social network can show up as gaps in the network, combined with the information of which people in the network search for those individuals allows the reconstruction of social graph.

characteristicExample.name: Contact lists
characteristicExample.description: Contact lists that are uploaded to services allow service providers to indirectly reconstruct the social graph of the involved individuals.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Many services rely on contact discovery to find other users on the service. Combining these contact lists from different individuals allows the service provider to reconstruct the social graph of the involved individuals.

impact.name: Construct profile
impact.description: The combination of records from multiple different sources enables building a more comprehensive profile on an individual.

criteria.name: Multiple users
criteria.description: Is data from multiple users combined?

criteria.name: Combine datasets
criteria.description: Are datasets or records combined?

additionalInformation.name: Data subject different from sender
additionalInformation.description: The data subject is not necessarily the sender of the data.

additionalInformation.name: Quasi-identifiers
additionalInformation.description: Quasi-identifiers can be sufficient to link and combine data from multiple users.

characteristic.name: Through Profiling, derivation, or inference
characteristic.description: Linking through derivation or inference
characteristic.fullDescription: Link different data items by deriving patterns from the data.

characteristic.name: Profiling an individual
characteristic.description: Personal data of an individual can be analyzed for patterns to link data to that individual. Association is performed at the basis of the data or user actions.

characteristicExample.name: Facial expression analysis
characteristicExample.description: By applying sentiment analysis to faces in pictures, the emotional state of an individual can be derived.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Sentiment analysis can be applied to faces in pictures to derive the emotional state of the individual in the photo. This type of sentiment recognition is applied by performing comparative analysis of one user against large datasets.

characteristicExample.name: Telemedicine e-health system
characteristicExample.description: The frequency of data exchanges from a health monitoring device allows an adversary to infer a patient's medical condition.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: By observing the frequency of the data exchanges from a health monitoring device, the adversary may learn or infer more about the medical condition of a patient: the more frequent data is exchanged, the more closely a patient is monitored, and the more serious their health condition.

characteristicExample.name: Requests to external services
characteristicExample.description: External service requests may be linked to the same user by inferring they are sent in the context of an ongoing session.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Requests to an external service may be tied to the same user by inferring that those requests are sent in the context of an ongoing session in which a user is currently involved.

characteristicExample.name: Personalized shopping recommendations
characteristicExample.description: Shopping recommendations sent to consumers are based on the degree of similarity to other consumers.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Many recommendation systems rely on constructing profiles of consumer purchases in order to make suggestions on other purchases.

impact.name: Link additional data
impact.description: Deriving patterns from the data can facilitate the linking of data that was not intended to be linked.

impact.name: Link requests
impact.description: Timing patterns of messages can be used to link requests to construct profiles.

impact.name: Indirectly reveal sensitive data
impact.description: Indirect links can reveal sensitive data about individuals that are not involved in the original dataset.

criteria.name: Data patterns
criteria.description: Are there patterns derivable from the data?
criteria.fullDescription: Are there patterns derivable from the data that can be used for linking multiple datasets or interactions together?

criteria.name: Inference through analyzing linked data
criteria.description: Can (new) personal data be inferred from the linked data points?
criteria.fullDescription: Can the linked data be used to infer additional information (including personal data) that was not a part of the original data set?

additionalInformation.name: Service usage
additionalInformation.description: The more data is collected and the more detailed it is, the easier it can become to discern patterns for linking.

characteristic.name: Profiling a group of individuals
characteristic.description: Data of a single individual leads to insights about a larger group of individuals. Knowledge transfers to other individuals through known relations of group membership or similarity.

characteristicExample.name: DNA testing service
characteristicExample.description: Findings obtained through DNA analysis (e.g., genetic predisposition for certain illnesses) by an individual may also apply to their family members.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: DNA analysis services process extremely sensitive data of not only the individual that submits their sample to the service. Because of the biological relationship, genetic information learned from their sample can also apply to family members.

characteristicExample.name: Energy consumption meter
characteristicExample.description: Readings obtained from an energy consumption meter do not apply to an individual but to households. Consumption patterns obtained for an individual (e.g. heating cost) may be generalized.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Readings obtained from an energy consumption meter do not apply to an individual but to households and in some cases (e.g. apartment buildings) to larger groups of individuals. Consumption patterns obtained for an individual (e.g. heating cost) may transfer to all building residents.

criteria.name: Generalize
criteria.description: Is there data being analyzed for patterns to generalize?

characteristic.name: Profiling an individual through (dis)similarity
characteristic.description: Applying methods to assess uniqueness or similarity to predict relevant properties.
characteristic.fullDescription: The application of learning methods that assess the uniqueness or similarity (clustering) of an individual enables prediction of relevant properties about an individual. Inference of membership of an individual in larger groups.

characteristicExample.name: Salary statistics queries
characteristicExample.description: Querying the average salary with a strict set of criteria can reveal the salary of an individual employee.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Querying the average salary from a database for employees with a strict set of criteria that only apply to a single individual reveals the actual salary of the individual employee.

characteristicExample.name: Through writing style
characteristicExample.description: Patterns in a person's writing style can be used to link multiple texts written by the same person.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Individuals have a particular writing style and use of expressions (e.g., whether they are a native speaker), this language patterns in the written text could be used to attribute different texts to the same author.

characteristicExample.name: Analyzing timing patterns
characteristicExample.description: Unique timing patterns could be recognized to link the use of a service to the same user.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: The timing patterns of when an individual connects to the service could be unique and used to link activity on the service to that particular individual.

characteristicExample.name: Analyzing messages
characteristicExample.description: Messages can be analyzed for patterns (e.g., writing style, timing) to link them to the same user.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Messages can be analyzed to derive patterns (e.g., in terms of writing style, timing) and link these messages to the same user.

impact.name: Construct profile
impact.description: When users are distinguishable from one another, user profiles can be constructed to collect growing amounts of personal data associated with each profile. This can later lead to `Identifying' threats.

criteria.name: Distinguishable
criteria.description: Is the data from different individuals distinguishable?

criteria.name: Queryable
criteria.description: Is it possible to query data using distinguishable attributes?

additionalInformation.name: Data without attributes
additionalInformation.description: Even data without clear attributes could contain patterns to allow distinguishing between different individuals.

impact.description: Linking becomes problematic when it can result in inference (learning more about individuals), singling out individuals, aggregating additional data to build profiles, etc. This may subsequently give rise to other threats, such as identifying.

additionalInformation.description: Linking refers to the process of associating different data items (incl. metadata) in a manner that results in undesirable privacy implications. Combining related data items may reveal (additional) information about a data subject or groups of data subjects.

threatType.name: Identifying
threatType.description: Identifying threats arise when the identity of individuals can be revealed through leaks, deduction, or inference in cases where this is not desired.
threatType.fullDescription: Personal data is by definition related to a data subject. Many systems may require identification of data subjects to meet their system goals. `Identifying' threats however express situations in which the identity of the data subject can be learned through leaks, can be deduced, or inferred when this is unwanted and to be prevented.

characteristic.name: Identified information
characteristic.description: Identified Information is requested or processed.
characteristic.fullDescription: Processing identified information in the system makes it trivial to obtain the identity of the affected individual.

characteristic.name: Processing of identified data
characteristic.description: The system requests and processes identified data
characteristic.fullDescription: The system requests and processes identified data about a data subject, either directly from the data subject or from a third party.

characteristicExample.name: Online service registration
characteristicExample.description: An online service requests full name and address during the registration process.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Many online services require extensive identity information during the registration (e.g., full name, address, phone numbers, etc.).

characteristicExample.name: Identification based on username
characteristicExample.description: The username for a service contains identity data (e.g., ``firstname.lastname'').
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Instead of a pseudonym (e.g, ``user93''), a username contains identity data (e.g., ``firstname.lastname''), this makes it trivial to determine the identity of the individual behind the account.

impact.name: Data breach amplification
impact.description: Identified data can severely amplify the impact of a future data breach.
impact.fullDescription: Requiring extensive personal data to use the system can severely amplify the impact of a future data breach.

impact.name: Reveal sensitive information about an individual
impact.description: Depending on the context, the identity may reveal very sensitive attributes (e.g., health records).
impact.fullDescription: Depending on the context of the system, the identity of the individual may reveal very sensitive attributes (e.g., system with people testing positive for certain medical condition).

criteria.name: Identifying Data
criteria.description: Does data sent to the system (potentially) contain identity data?

additionalInformation.name: Require identification
additionalInformation.description: Users often need to provide identified data even when not essential for the functionality.
additionalInformation.fullDescription: Users are forced to provide identifying data while not required for the requested functionality.

additionalInformation.name: Strong measures
additionalInformation.description: Identified data requires stronger security measures.

characteristic.name: Identified information in metadata
characteristic.description: The metadata of files or communication involves identified information.
characteristic.fullDescription: Even in data exchanges that do not directly contain identified information, the identity of the data subject may be established based on identified information included in metadata or contextual data.

characteristicExample.name: Author information in document metadata
characteristicExample.description: A software product for authoring documents may automatically insert author information in the metadata of the produced documents.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Many software products for authoring documents include authorship information in the document metadata and in exported variants such as pdfs. While such information can be useful during document authoring and reviewing, it could be undesirable in the final outputs.

impact.name: Unintentional identification
impact.description: The presence of identifying data in metadata may lead to the unintentional identification of a data subject.

criteria.name: Metadata
criteria.description: Does the system process data that has metadata associated with it?

criteria.name: Identified information in metadata
criteria.description: Does the associated metadata contain identified information?

characteristic.name: Identifiable information
characteristic.description: The system processes identifiable information from which the identity of the data subject may be derived.
characteristic.fullDescription: This characteristic groups together all types of derivations that in theory could lead to the identity of the data subject.

characteristic.name: Pseudonym
characteristic.description: The data contains unique references to the identity of the data subject.
characteristic.fullDescription: When data is pseudonymized, the data is linked to a single data subject through a pseudonym. The combined data linked to that individual may be sufficient to obtain the identity of that individual.

characteristic.name: Identifier
characteristic.description: The data contains a unique reference to the identity of the data subject.
characteristic.fullDescription: When data has a unique reference, the data is linked to a single data subject through a pseudonym.

characteristicExample.name: Online service username
characteristicExample.description: The (re)use of an email address facilitates easy combination with other data, leading to the identification of the individual.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: The (re)use of unique identifiers, such as email addresses, in online services makes it trivial the combine it with other data held for the same individual and enables identifying that individual.

characteristicExample.name: IP addresses
characteristicExample.description: IP addresses in communication can be used to uniquely identify an individual.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: IP addresses are frequently related to particular individuals. Parties such as Internet service providers know exactly who the individual is behind those addresses. Other parties could determine this through linking with other activity from that IP address.

characteristicExample.name: Insufficient de-identification
characteristicExample.description: Globally unique identifiers (e.g., SSN) are replaced by internal ids. These are still tied to the actual identity.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: While replacing globally unique identifiers by internal IDs makes the identifying less straightforward, the data is still all related to one particular individual and any party that is able to obtain or infer the mapping can identify them.

impact.name: De-anonymize
impact.description: Pseudonyms facilitate the aggregation of data on the same individual (see linking). Storing a substantial amount of data increases the possibility of identifying the individual behind it.

criteria.name: Pseudonym used
criteria.description: Is there a distinctive identifier used during interactions or when referring to an individual's data?
criteria.fullDescription: Is a pseudonym used in interactions with the system or when referring to data of an individual?

characteristic.name: Quasi-identifier
characteristic.description: The data contains combinations of attributes that are unique to a data subject.
characteristic.fullDescription: The combination of attributes may serve as a pseudonym for data relating to a data subject and could together be used to establish the identity of the data subject.

characteristicExample.name: Browser fingerprint
characteristicExample.description: Browser fingerprinting entails the combination of various properties to create a unique identifier, serving as a pseudonym for the user.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: A browser communicates several details about its capabilities to the websites that it visits. This information can be sufficiently unique to serve as a pseudonym for a particular user that combined with a login or other data could lead to identifying the user.

characteristicExample.name: Dataset with quasi-identifiers
characteristicExample.description: A dataset removes names and reduces addresses to cities. Nevertheless, a combination of various attributes (city, birth date, language preference, etc.) could still be adequate to identify individuals.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: In a dataset, certain attributes could be removed or abstracted such as removing names and reducing addresses to cities. However, depending on the context of that dataset, combinations of different attributes may still be enough to serve as a pseudonym for particular individuals and could lead, combined with other information, to the identification of the individual.

criteria.name: Quasi-identifier
criteria.description: Can multiple attributes be combined to create a unique reference to an individual or their data?

additionalInformation.name: Identifier reuse
additionalInformation.description: Identifying individuals through identifiers is easy when these identifiers are reused across multiple services or in publicly available data.

characteristic.name: Revealing attributes
characteristic.description: A number of revealing attributes are included in the data which support the identification of the data subject.
characteristic.fullDescription: A set of different attributes relating to an individual may be provided to the system. While those attributes may individually appear harmless, combining them could be more revealing and lead to the identification of the data subject.

characteristicExample.name: Feedback form
characteristicExample.description: When an individual shares detailed data (such as location, employer, device type, etc.) in a feedback form, the provided information may be revealing enough to uniquely identify that person.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: In a feedback form that receives free text input, the data and particular details in that data could be sufficient to reveal the identity of the individual providing the feedback. For example, if the feedback concerns functionality that was only released to a small set of beta-testers in different application domains, the combination of that functionality, together with a particular use case in which the individual is experiencing a problem, could be sufficient to identify that user.

impact.name: Accidentally revealing identity
impact.description: Inadvertently providing identifiable attributes in user-submitted data can lead to the unintentional identification of the individual.

criteria.name: User provided inputs
criteria.description: Is there free-form user provided data that is received or processed by the system?

criteria.name: Revealing data
criteria.description: Is data collected that may reveal the identifying information?

additionalInformation.name: Data subject
additionalInformation.description: The data subject is not necessarily the source of the provided data.

characteristic.name: The data subject is distinguishable from others
characteristic.description: The anonymity set is too small, which allows singling out an individual data subject.
characteristic.fullDescription: The data subject may become distinguishable through the data that is shared, but also through metadata, participation in communication, behavior in the system, etc.

characteristicExample.name: Individual queries
characteristicExample.description: User search queries, such as looking up nearby businesses or info about a rare illness, can be highly specific and may lead to identification.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Search queries of a user may be very specific to that particular individual. For example looking up information about a business nearby or information about a particular illness. Those queries can be very different from those of other users, making it possible to identify users.

characteristicExample.name: Distinguishable website visitor
characteristicExample.description: A person's consistent access at a particular time each week could link their visits even when they are not logged into their account.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: An e-shop tracks a user's access. John Doe accesses the website every Monday around 10PM (but only sporadically purchases something). Even when John is not logged in, the shop can identify John based on his contextual data (with a certain likelihood).

characteristicExample.name: Gait recognition
characteristicExample.description: An individual's gait can be used to uniquely identify them.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: The analysis of an individual's gait (the manner or style of walking) can be used to extract a number of features that can be combined to uniquely identify the individual.

characteristicExample.name: Queries with small resultset
characteristicExample.description: Queries with a very small result set could deliver results unique to a particular individual.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Queries can be constructed that return a very small result set, to the extent that the query results can be tied to a unique individual.

characteristicExample.name: Biometric authentication
characteristicExample.description: Authentication with biometrics (e.g., fingerprint or iris) work based on being able to uniquely link these biometric properties to a single user.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Authentication systems that leverage biometrics rely on the fact that this biometric data is very specific to particular individuals. This can make it easy to identify particular individuals.

characteristicExample.name: Face recognition
characteristicExample.description: The use of facial recognition processing on, for example, profile images can enable the derivation of attributes that can be combined to identify the depicted individual.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Facial recognition can be used to identify the same individual in a different picture, combined with additional context information about those pictures could lead to the identification of users.

impact.name: Reveal identity
impact.description: Even without identity information, user actions or data may be very specific and unintentionally reveal the identity.

criteria.name: Uniqueness
criteria.description: Are requests or records sufficiently unique to differentiate them from those of a specific individual?

additionalInformation.name: Likelihood
additionalInformation.description: The likelihood depends on how distinguishable an individual is from others.

impact.description: It can be undesirable to know the identity. Working with identified data records requires additional protective measures and can lead to other threats such as unawareness and non-compliance.

additionalInformation.description: A key distinction is made between threats in the context of identified data (where there is an explicit link), and identifiable data (where the link can be derived based on a pseudonym, identity-revealing content, or a small set of potential subjects, known as the anonymity set, that allow (re-)identification).

threatType.name: Non-repudiation
threatType.description: Non-repudiation threats pertain to situations where an individual can no longer deny specific claims.
threatType.fullDescription:
Non-repudiation threats represent outcomes in which an individual is not able to deny certain claims specifically about their involvement in the system, or more broadly any claim pertaining themselves, as a consequence of the data collected, shared or an action taken by the individual (or other individuals) in the system.
Non-repudiation threats for a claim involve two key elements: (i) the system maintains evidence or proof of a fact or action related to an individual, impacting the plausible deniability (e.g., logfiles from an involved party that could be tampered with, or digital signatures providing strong guarantees of the authenticity of the evidence), (ii) that evidence is attributable to an individual. Both evidences can have varying strength which will result in a varying non-repudiation threat impact

characteristic.name: Attributable data evidence
characteristic.description: A data record or message is (or can be) attributed to a user or data subject.
characteristic.fullDescription: The data itself can impact deniability claims.

characteristic.name: Data
characteristic.description: Data can be used to prevent an individual from denying certain claims.
characteristic.fullDescription: Data that is kept in an accessible form could be used as evidence to prevent an individual from denying certain claims with regard to the data or what is described in the data.

characteristicExample.name: Logged transmissions
characteristicExample.description: Transmissions are logged as evidence of communication.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Systems that log the transmission of messages can provide evidence that certain messages were sent. This may be undesirable if users should have plausible deniability of their communication.

characteristicExample.name: Random data could indicate encryption
characteristicExample.description: Random data could be an indication that there is encrypted data, especially if it concerns the full drive or external device.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: When a complete disk or external storage drive is full of random data, this could be a strong indication that the drive is encrypted. As it is unlikely to just be a drive full of random data. Given the likelihood of the encryption, this could lead to forced key disclosure.

characteristicExample.name: Encrypted office document
characteristicExample.description: An encrypted office document still has the office file format, but requires a password to open it. This document format makes it clear that there is encrypted data.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: If the encryption preserves the file format (for example, an encrypted office document), it removes any plausible deniability about the fact that there is encrypted data there.

characteristicExample.name: Credentials
characteristicExample.description: An account with a corporate email address eliminates the employee's deniability of having used that service.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: If employees use their corporate email address to sign up for a service, their employer may have evidence of their use of those services in their mail logs.

characteristicExample.name: Corporate email address
characteristicExample.description: The use of a corporate mail address makes it impossible to deny being affiliated with that organization.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: If an employee signs up a with a corporate email address for a service, they can no longer plausibly deny being affiliated with that organization, since they have an active email account with them.

characteristicExample.name: Admin access logs
characteristicExample.description: System administrators can access log files linking an entry in an internal complaint system to the individual employee.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Administrators could have broad access to the logs of many internal organizational systems. This allows those administrators to tie employee submissions or registrations in internal systems to the particular individuals having performed them, thereby removing the plausible deniability of those employees.

impact.name: Identifying information amplification.
impact.description: Identity information can magnify the impact.

impact.name: Service context
impact.description: Depending on the context (e.g., medical, whistleblower), this can have a large impact on the data subject.

criteria.name: Record data impacting deniability
criteria.description: Does the system record data affecting deniability?
criteria.fullDescription: Is there data describing something that requires plausible deniability by a data subject.

criteria.name: Data impacting deniability
criteria.description: Does the data itself impact deniability claims?

additionalInformation.name: Data selection
additionalInformation.description: If deniability is required, do not store the data at all or remove any attributable data.

additionalInformation.name: Credentials
additionalInformation.description: Avoid credentials with identity information.

characteristic.name: Signed data
characteristic.description: Signed data can prevent deniability.
characteristic.fullDescription: Digital signatures by an individual or a trusted third party provide a strong source of evidence that prevents deniability claims as third parties can independently verify these signatures.

characteristicExample.name: Digital signatures
characteristicExample.description: A digitally signed email prevents the user from later denying having written the message.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Digital signatures attached to emails provide a strong form of evidence of the user having written the email message, thereby removing their plausible deniability about having written it.

characteristicExample.name: DKIM
characteristicExample.description: A common spam countermeasure (DKIM) involves signing outgoing emails, this prevents users from denying the authenticity of leaked or stolen emails.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: DKIM stands for `DomainKeys Identified Mail' and is a common countermeasure in the fight against spam. DKIM works by having an email provider, such as GMail, sign all outgoing emails to provide proof that they were sent from their servers, and publishing the signing key in a DNS record to enable anyone to verify the legitimacy of a sent emails. However, as a side-effect, this mechanism builds strong evidence (a digital signature by the E-mail provider) and links this evidence to the individual having sent the message (represented by the sender E-mail address in the signed message). This thus reduces plausible deniability of having sent an email.

characteristicExample.name: Blockchain storage
characteristicExample.description: Data stored on a blockchain cannot be modified, eliminating the deniability of claims related to this data.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Distributed ledgers, such as blockchains, prevent modifications of data on the chain. This provides a strong historic record which cannot be altered and thus prevents future deniability claims.

impact.name: Prevent deniability
impact.description: Signatures provide strong non-repudiation, as they can also be verified by third parties.

impact.name: append-only storage
impact.description: Append-only storage systems make it impossible for the data subject to later remove their personal data.

criteria.name: Digitally signed
criteria.description: Is the data digitally signed?

criteria.name: Signing keys
criteria.description: Which keys are used for signing? Who has access to these keys to verify signatures?

additionalInformation.name: Requests
additionalInformation.description: Signed data applies not only to messages, but also to documents, requests, etc.

characteristic.name: Metadata
characteristic.description: Metadata can contain unintended data impacting deniability claims about that data.
characteristic.fullDescription: Many transmission protocols and file formats include several metadata fields that may contain additional data that was not intended to be included and that could impact the deniability of claims regarding that data.

characteristicExample.name: Document metadata
characteristicExample.description: Author or revision metadata in documents prevents deniability.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Many document authoring software products include authorship and revision information in the document metadata. This information can make it impossible for individuals to later deny involvement in creating or revising a particular document.

impact.name: Unintentional metadata impacting deniability
impact.description: The unintentional inclusion of metadata with data or transmissions may impact deniability claims.

criteria.name: Presence of metadata
criteria.description: Does stored or transmitted data have associated metadata?

characteristic.name: Embedded/Hidden Data
characteristic.description: Embedded or hidden data can be used to reveal additional information impacting deniability claims about the data.
characteristic.fullDescription: Data may contain hidden or embedded patterns that enable attributing the data to a specific individual. Such attributions impact deniability claims where an individual needs plausible deniability with regard to the data.

characteristicExample.name: Watermarked Data
characteristicExample.description: Data watermarked with hidden artifacts (uniquely linked to a person) can be used to track the person revealing or disclosing the data afterwards.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Documents or media could be watermarked with information tied to a particular individual in order to prevent sharing or disclosing that data to others. The information hidden in the data could later be used to determine who distributed the information and thus impacting their deniability claims. This could be used to prosecute or punish whistleblowers that share internal information.

characteristicExample.name: Embedded remote resources
characteristicExample.description: Remote resources (e.g. image in email) are automatically loaded to track the user opening it.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Remote resources could be automatically loaded (e.g. a link to an image in an email), and this may be used to log the action of opening of a message or file.

characteristicExample.name: Custom secrets
characteristicExample.description: Secrets shared with one person, or modified for each recipient can serve as evidence of the disclosure of that data by that person.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: As a variant on document watermarks, the information or content itself could be slightly modified for each intended recipient to be able to determine which recipient shared the data with others.

impact.name: Hidden data impacting deniability claims
impact.description: Hidden/embedded data can prevent a user from denying claims about the data.
impact.fullDescription: The presence of hidden or embedded data can reveal information impacting deniability claims about the data.

criteria.name: Embedded data
criteria.description: Are there embedded data or hidden patterns in the data or transmissions?

criteria.name: Embedded or metadata causes deniability issues
criteria.description: Does this data lead to undesirable deniability issues?

additionalInformation.name: Active countermeasure
additionalInformation.description: This is also used as an explicit countermeasure to prevent people from sharing data.

characteristic.name: Attributable action side-effect evidence
characteristic.description: Action side-effects can cause an action to be attributable to an individual.
characteristic.fullDescription: Some actions in the system can trigger side-effects that make the execution of an action attributable to an individual impacting their plausible deniability.

characteristicExample.name: Read notifications
characteristicExample.description: Read notifications serve as evidence that the user has opened/read the message.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: If a messaging application automatically sends `message read' notifications to senders, the recipient no longer has any plausible deniability of having read the message.

characteristicExample.name: Browser history
characteristicExample.description: An individual's browser history may be used to substantiate claims about their online activities.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: The browser history provides evidence of websites that were visited before by the user. The cached resources can also speed up the loading of resources, this provides evidence that certain sites were previously visited.

characteristicExample.name: Action logging
characteristicExample.description: Actions can be logged as evidence.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: The actions a user performs in an application could all be logged to provide evidence of everything the user has done.

impact.name: Action side-effect impacting deniability
impact.description: Some actions may trigger side-effects that impact deniability claims regarding those actions.

criteria.name: Action side-effects
criteria.description: Do (passive) interactions with the system (e.g., receiving a message) have side-effects (e.g., trigger transmissions, logging)?

criteria.name: Deniable action
criteria.description: Is deniability of receipt a desired feature for the system?

additionalInformation.name: Implicit
additionalInformation.description: These side-effects often happen implicitly or without user intervention.

impact.description: Non-repudiation threats impact the plausible deniability of individuals, rendering them unable to refute specific actions or involvements, such as submitting a whistleblower report or casting a vote for someone.

additionalInformation.description: The system retains evidence related to a particular action or fact, influencing the ability to deny claims. Examples of this evidence include log files, digital signatures, document metadata, and watermarked data, all of which can be attributed to an individual.

threatType.name: Detecting
threatType.description: Detecting threats pertain to situations where the involvement, participation, or membership of an individual can be deduced through observation.
threatType.fullDescription:
Detecting threats represent cases of becoming aware of data subject involvement, membership, or participation to the system by observing existence of relevant information, through (i) observed communication, (ii) observed application side-effects (e.g., temporary files in the file system), or (iii) through system responses that may give away information about the existence of these elements. This final case addressed both threats caused by adversaries trying to probe the system (i.e., evoke responses that give away information about existence of data records), or system responses that accidentally leak information about the existence of specific records.
It is important to note that detecting threats do not require access to the data itself. Being able to observe existing of stored data, side-effects of processes, or communication flows between certain parties can be sufficient to deduce additional relevant information about an individual.
These threats involve an active threat actor, such as a receiving party that can deduce more information than they were suppose to, an outsider who observes the communication channel, or an insider (e.g. employee with internal access).

characteristic.name: Observed communications
characteristic.description: Detecting through observed communications
characteristic.fullDescription: Detection occurs through observing communications between (sub)systems: the existence or lack thereof, or patterns within the observed communications.

characteristicExample.name: Infer user of a website
characteristicExample.description: Observing communication with a service to infer that a person is a user (e.g., adult website).
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Even if the traffic to a certain website is encrypted, detecting the existence of that traffic to the website is enough to infer that a particular individual is a user of that website.

characteristicExample.name: Telemedicine e-health system
characteristicExample.description: Communication with a telemedicine service implies the user is a patient.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: In a telemedicine system, by monitoring communication volume, frequency or patterns between a health device and a health gateway, an adversary may gather useful information. Simply the existence of a health device may imply that the user living at home is a registered patient.

characteristicExample.name: Tor network participant
characteristicExample.description: Participation in the Tor network can be determined by observing traffic.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: An observer may intercept and recognize Tor network traffic but has no way to distinguish whether or not a participant is actively using the network or if it is just acting as a proxy/intermediate node in the Tor network. Detection of participation is possible, but the specific role or nature of this participation can not be detected.

characteristicExample.name: Wireless transmissions
characteristicExample.description: Wireless transmissions are detectable by other devices nearby.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Wireless communication methods involve broadcasting the data to other wireless receivers. Even if the transmitted data is encrypted, other wireless receivers can still detect the wireless transmissions and their signal strength.

impact.name: Sensitive context
impact.description: In sensitive contexts (medical, whistleblower) detecting service usage may have a severe impact on the user.

criteria.name: Detectable communications
criteria.description: Can the communication be observed?

criteria.name: Relevant communications
criteria.description: Can information be inferred from the observed communications?

additionalInformation.name: Tor
additionalInformation.description: Services like Tor conceal the destination but the utilization of Tor can still be detected.

characteristic.name: Application side effect
characteristic.description: Detecting through (trans)action side effects
characteristic.fullDescription: Application actions or transactions may have side effects at which basis detection may occur.

characteristicExample.name: System logs
characteristicExample.description: Log files on a shared system reveal applications used or actions taken by other users.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: A user logged into a shared system may simply consult log files to see the side-effects or outputs of applications executed by different users. This way, he may derive which applications are used by a different user, which in turn may be the basis of disclosure of additional information about these different users.

characteristicExample.name: Deleted application
characteristicExample.description: Deleted applications may leave behind traces (configuration, temporary files).
characteristicExample.fullDescription: A deleted application on a smartphone may leave behind a trail of configuration files, temporary files, etc, which can be used by an external adversary (e.g., inspecting the phone's storage volumes) to identify which applications and services are used by the phone owner.

characteristicExample.name: Hidden data
characteristicExample.description: When steganography is used to hide data, the increased file size may still indicate the existence of that hidden data.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Using steganography, relevant data may be hidden within other data records. However, data may not be well-hidden, in the sense that it may influence the carrier of the information in a way that is detectable. For example, a picture with an excessive file size may reveal that additional information is contained therein.

characteristicExample.name: Detecting content tracing test result communication
characteristicExample.description: A user reporting a positive test result in a contact tracing app may trigger observable communication that discloses medical information.

impact.name: Infer sensitive data
impact.description: Sensitive information may be deduced from observed side effects, such as communication.

criteria.name: Action side effects
criteria.description: Do actions in the system have side effects (e.g., saving a file, writing to a log, triggering other transmissions)?

criteria.name: Detectable side effects
criteria.description: Are these side effects observable?

additionalInformation.name: Dummy traffic
additionalInformation.description: Dummy traffic can be used to conceal actual events.

characteristic.name: System responses
characteristic.description: The existence of an item of interest is revealed in a system response (which can be evoked deliberately or given accidentally).

characteristicExample.name: Wrong password
characteristicExample.description: A `wrong password' error message reveals the existence of the account.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: When a system provides an incorrect password message, it reveals the existence of an account with the provided username or email address. A better response would be to limit the information to just `incorrect credentials' as this could either be an incorrect password or an non-existing user account.

characteristicExample.name: Firewall
characteristicExample.description: A firewall responding with `port closed' reveals the existence of a device at the IP address.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: A firewall that responds with a closed port rather than ignoring the communication reveals the existence of a device at the targeted IP address.

characteristicExample.name: DB access denied
characteristicExample.description: An error message stating `insufficient access rights' may inadvertently leak the existence of a specific record.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: An error message informing the user about insufficient access rights may leak information about the existence or non-existence of specific records in the system.

characteristicExample.name: Bounced email
characteristicExample.description: The existence of email accounts can be inferred from bounced emails.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: By attempting to send an email to an unknown or suspected mail user and observing whether or not the mail server bounces (i.e., returns the sent mail with a message that the recipient is unknown), the adversary may derive that a certain mail address is in use, and thus that the targeted mail recipient is in fact a registered mail user.

characteristicExample.name: Address already registered
characteristicExample.description: An error message stating `address already registered' when subscribing to a political newsletter reveals a current member.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: When the system to subscribe to, for example a newsletter, provides an error message that the address is already registered, it reveals the existence of an address in the subscriber list.

characteristicExample.name: Cached browser resources
characteristicExample.description: To speed up the loading of websites, browsers can provide certain remote resources from their local cache. This enables detecting which resources were already cached.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Browsers perform several optimizations to improve the performance. To speed up the loading of webpages, remote resources can be provided from the local browser cache rather than downloading them again from a remote server. However, the time difference in loading these resources could be used for detecting that those resources are in the browser cache, and the user has thus visited pages that load them before.

impact.name: Detecting can lead to security threats
impact.description: Being able to detect the existence of certain items can be a stepping stone to security threats.

impact.name: Existence
impact.description: Simply knowing the existence of data may be sufficient to infer sensitive information.

criteria.name: Status messages
criteria.description: Does the system show status messages (informational, warnings, errors) when retrieving data?

criteria.name: Status reveals existence
criteria.description: Are the status messages distinct when an item (a file, user, ...) does not exist compared to not having access rights?

additionalInformation.name: Redesign system response
additionalInformation.description: Prevent information leakage by not revealing the existence of items in system responses.

impact.description: Observing or ascertaining the existence can be sufficient to learn sensitive information about individuals. Furthermore, detecting also facilitates linking and identifying, allowing for the inference of additional information about individuals.

additionalInformation.description: Detecting can be done by observing communication flows, including interactions with a system or service, and communication between systems. Detecting can also be achieved by observing application side effects or system responses, where the existence of certain data may be inadvertently revealed by the system.

threatType.name: Data Disclosure
threatType.description: Data disclosure threats represent cases in which disclosures of personal data to, within, and from the system are considered problematic.
threatType.fullDescription:
A data disclosure is the transfer of personal data across a boundary, i.e. the collection of data by the system or the transfer of data to a known or unknown third party. From a privacy perspective, these disclosures should take into account the best interest of the involved data subjects. The minimality principle is key here. Only collect, process, store and share the strictly required personal data. Data disclosure threats represent cases in which disclosure of personal data is considered problematic. More precisely, `Data Disclosure' threats represent cases in which either the explicit (i.e. intended or designed) or the implicit (i.e. unintended or consequential) disclosure of personal data is considered avoidable.
When disclosures happen intentionally and by design (i.e. the system collects personal data to perform its functional goals) it is considered explicit. Conversely, disclosures are deemed implicit when they are indirect (i.e. through metadata or derived from other data that is disclosed).

characteristic.name: Unnecessary data types
characteristic.description: Depending on the context, data can be perceived highly sensitive, and should therefore only be collected and processed when strictly required.

characteristic.name: Data type sensitivity
characteristic.description: More sensitive data types are collected than functionally required by the system.

characteristicExample.name: Patient health monitoring
characteristicExample.description: Tracking a patient's weight is pertinent for dieting apps but not for a contact tracing application.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: A medical application that assesses the health status of a patient will often not need to collect all possible medical parameters of a patient but only those useful for monitoring the targeted disease or pathology. For example, recording patient weight will be relevant in the context of a dieting app or an app used during pregnancy, but it will not be relevant in a contact tracing application.

impact.name: Amplify data breach impact
impact.description: Processing excessively sensitive data amplifies the impact of a potential data breach, thereby increasing the consequences for the affected individuals.

criteria.name: Sensitivity
criteria.description: Is the data more sensitive than strictly necessary?

additionalInformation.name: Consider necessity
additionalInformation.description: When designing the system, assess whether all the data is genuinely necessary for providing the system's functionality.

characteristic.name: Data type granularity
characteristic.description: Disclosed personal data is of a more fine-grained level of granularity than needed.

characteristicExample.name: Smart meter
characteristicExample.description: A smart meter shares realtime measurements rather than the aggregated consumption.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: A smart meter can locally process the household consumption and share an aggregated overview to the back-end system, rather than sharing detailed measurements.

criteria.name: Granularity
criteria.description: Is the data more fine-grained than strictly necessary?

characteristic.name: Data type encoding
characteristic.description: The encoding of the data includes additional personal data that is not functionally needed.

characteristicExample.name: Camera app
characteristicExample.description: A camera application on a smartphone does not necessarily need to record the picture's location.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Camera applications on smartphones can also use location services to include record location information in pictures that were taken. This is not always necessary and could be problematic when users share pictures taken in their home.

characteristicExample.name: Geo-tagged photos
characteristicExample.description: The transmission of geo-tagged pictures also includes location data of the individual that took the pictures.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: When geo-tagged pictures are taken, the picture's metadata also includes location information. Sharing or transmitting these pictures to online services can expose the user's physical location.

characteristicExample.name: Metadata
characteristicExample.description: Documents processed may automatically include metadata that contain personal data such as the author or reviewer of a document.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Many document authoring programs include author and reviewer data in the document metadata.

criteria.name: Encoding
criteria.description: Does the data encoding include additional (meta)data?

characteristic.name: Excessive volume
characteristic.description: The characteristic involves the volume of personal data that is collected and processed.

characteristic.name: Amount
characteristic.description: An excessive amount of personal data is processed beyond what is functionally needed.

characteristicExample.name: Data subject age
characteristicExample.description: A generic service that is not age-restricted should not request a user's age.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: An online service requests a lot of user information when registering, while none of this information is required for providing the functionality of the service.

criteria.name: Amount
criteria.description: Is the amount of collected data necessary for the correct functioning of the system?

characteristic.name: Frequency
characteristic.description: Personal data is processed more frequently than functionally needed.

characteristicExample.name: Patient weight recording
characteristicExample.description: Recording patient weight on a weekly or monthly basis may suffice; collecting such information every half hour is unnecessary.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: It may be necessary only to record patient weight on a weekly or monthly basis, and collecting such information every half hour is considered unnecessary, given that these apps track weight evolutions over longer periods of time.

impact.name: Frequent collection
impact.description: Regular data collection results in an increased dataset, potentially giving rise to additional privacy threats, such as data mining for patterns.

criteria.name: Frequency
criteria.description: Is the processing frequency necessary?

additionalInformation.name: Consider frequency
additionalInformation.description: Evaluate whether regular data collection is necessary for the system's functionality.

characteristic.name: Involved data subjects
characteristic.description: Personal data is processed of more data subjects than functionally needed.

characteristicExample.name: Posting on social networks
characteristicExample.description: Posts on social networks frequently include personal data about other individuals.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Social media posts frequently include mentions of other people or pictures that include others. This involves additional people in the processing of personal data and is not always necessary.

criteria.name: Number of data subjects
criteria.description: Are there more data subjects involved than necessary?

characteristic.name: Unnecessary processing
characteristic.description: This characteristic considers whether the processing and treatment of the personal data is actually necessary for achieving the functional goals of the system.

characteristic.name: Treatment, analysis, enrichment, transformation
characteristic.description: Personal data is further treated, analyzed, and enriched in a way that is not necessary to achieve the functionality of the system.

characteristicExample.name: Face recognition, emotion detection
characteristicExample.description: A camera application on a smartphone does not need to perform face-based recognition or emotion detection.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: A camera application of a smartphone does not necessarily need to perform face-based recognition or emotion detection, unless these are directly motivated by the functional goals of the system.

characteristicExample.name: Text analysis
characteristicExample.description: Analyzing a user's blog posts for language proficiency is unnecessary for blogging functionality.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Stylometry can be applied to written language in order to automatically derive the author's mother tongue or calculate a language proficiency score. This type of analysis should not be performed unless it is strictly required to meet functional system goals.

characteristicExample.name: Constructing profiles on individuals
characteristicExample.description: User profiles accumulate unnecessary details over time, tracking a broad range of actions or service usage that is not essential for the provided functionality.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: User profiles accumulate and grow over time, keeping track of a wide range of actions or service usage. The accumulation and retention of rich and detailed profiles may not be functionally required.

characteristicExample.name: Facial expression analysis
characteristicExample.description: Sentiment analysis can be applied to faces in pictures to derive the emotional state of the individual in the photo.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Systems can perform advanced processing on photos to detect faces and analyze the facial expressions. This type of analysis should not be performed unless it is strictly required to meet functional system goals.

impact.name: Processing can increase sensitivity
impact.description: Processing the data can be used to learn additional sensitive information.

criteria.name: Data enrichment
criteria.description: Is the data enrichment/analysis necessary for the system's functionality?

additionalInformation.name: Consider processing
additionalInformation.description: Evaluate which types of personal data processing are necessary for providing the system's functionality.

characteristic.name: Propagation
characteristic.description: Data is accessible by or propagated to other services where it is not needed.

characteristicExample.name: Propagation of location data
characteristicExample.description: Location data from a navigation application is propagated to all the other applications (e.g., calendar, mail).
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Location data collected by a navigation application is propagated to all the other applications and services such as calendar, mail, and other apps.

criteria.name: Recipient necessity
criteria.description: Is the data necessary for the recipient?

characteristic.name: Implicit data disclosure
characteristic.description: Data is implicitly collected as a side-effect of explicit data disclosures or data flows.
characteristic.fullDescription: Data is implicitly collected as a side-effect of explicit data disclosures or data flows through, for example, patterns or frequencies of these flows. These implicit data flows and disclosures must be investigated

characteristicExample.name: Service usage
characteristicExample.description: Data gathered on the usage of a service (such as connection times or durations).
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Many systems collect detailed information about the usage of services and particular functionality. When this is recorded at the level of individual users it implicitly discloses a lot of additional information such as, for example, working hours.

criteria.name: Implicit data
criteria.description: Do service usage (patterns) reveal user data?

characteristic.name: Duration/retention
characteristic.description: Personal data is processed or kept longer than functionally needed.

characteristicExample.name: Retaining newsletter subscriber addresses
characteristicExample.description: Retaining the email addresses of newsletter subscribers long after they have unsubscribed.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Retaining the email addresses of newsletter subscribers long after they have unsubscribed. They serve no further purpose and increase the impact of a potential data breach.

impact.name: Storing data longer than needed
impact.description: Storing data longer than needed serves no further purpose and increases the impact of a data breach.

criteria.name: Duration
criteria.description: Is the data stored for longer time than necessary?

additionalInformation.name: Consider storage policies
additionalInformation.description: Evaluate your storage policies. Consider how long you store personal data and whether you have a process to remove data you no longer need.

characteristic.name: Involved parties and exposure
characteristic.description: Personal data is excessively exposed, either to external parties known and anticipated at design time (which are typically limited, targeted and scoped), or it is published or broadcasted by the system (which greatly amplifies the potential risk).

characteristic.name: Involved parties
characteristic.description: Personal data made accessible to more parties than functionally necessary.

characteristic.name: Predetermined set of parties
characteristic.description: The parties with whom personal data is shared are known up front. This set of parties is static and fixed.

characteristicExample.name: Sharing data to advertisers
characteristicExample.description: In a health application, even if collecting patient weight data is considered necessary, sharing this data with third party advertisers is unnecessary and harmful.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Many online services integrate with a lot of different third parties (for example, for advertising). When health applications collect patient health data, this data should not be shared with advertisers as it is unnecessary and harmful.

characteristicExample.name: Use of third party tracking and analytics services
characteristicExample.description: Using third party tracking and analytics services on websites involves transferring personal data about the user and their site usage to third parties.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Third party tracking and analytics services entail the transmission of personal data of the user to these third parties.

characteristicExample.name: Third party email delivery
characteristicExample.description: When using third party service providers for email delivery, personal data (e.g. about sender and recipients) is directly shared with these third parties.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: When using a third party email delivery service, all email communications (both metadata and contents) are shared with this third party.

characteristicExample.name: Speech data
characteristicExample.description: Speech data sent to a third party transcription service can apart from speech content reveal additional information about the individual such as mother tongue, gender, etc.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Services that need to perform speech processing (for example, for transcriptions) can rely on third parties to provide this functionality. As this involves the transmission of speech data, this data can also reveal additional information about the individuals such as their mother tongue, gender, emotions, number of people in household (through background noise), etc.

criteria.name: Involved parties
criteria.description: Are there more parties involved than necessary?

characteristic.name: Dynamic set of parties
characteristic.description: The parties with whom personal data is shared are determined dynamically and may change frequently.

characteristicExample.name: Shared with users
characteristicExample.description: Personal data is disclosed to other users of the service.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Personal data of an individual may be shared with other users of the service. For example, it may be accessible to employees or other users of a service.

criteria.name: Involved parties
criteria.description: Are there more parties involved than necessary?

criteria.name: Involved parties
criteria.description: Are there more parties involved than necessary?

characteristic.name: Availability/accessibility of data
characteristic.description: Personal data is published more broadly than necessary.

characteristicExample.name: Publishing research datasets
characteristicExample.description: In a medical application, while collecting patient weight data is deemed necessary, making such datasets publicly available would be unnecessary and harmful.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: While it can be useful to share datasets for research and analysis; not all data should be made publicly available. Care should be taken to ensure which types of data are released.

characteristicExample.name: Doxing
characteristicExample.description: Posting personal data of other people to publicly shame them, extort them, or trigger vigilante attacks, etc.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Online services that allow people to publicly post information could be used maliciously to broadcast the personal data of other individuals and violate their privacy.

characteristicExample.name: Phone number search
characteristicExample.description: Searching user by phone number can be used to discover/confirm someone else's phone number.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Functionality that enables looking up people through phone numbers could be used to guess or confirm that information.

characteristicExample.name: Lookup company founding data
characteristicExample.description: The original publication of a company's foundation reveals the home addresses of the founders.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Government registers of company registration records could provide personal details on its founders such as their private home address.

characteristicExample.name: Query interface reveals personal data
characteristicExample.description: Query interfaces to searcj for people working in specific area, may reveal their location of employment.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: A query interface may give up personal data of an individual. For example, searching for people working in a specific area may not only reveal those individuals, but also their location of employment. This information could be revealed if the results are based on this information, even if they have not made the information itself public.

characteristicExample.name: Sending private messages over a social network
characteristicExample.description: Posting private messages to a person through a social network in a public forum that may be seen and monitored my many.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: Messages sent through a social network between individuals may not necessarily be private. Depending on the social network settings, those messages could be discoverable or readable by others.

characteristicExample.name: Collecting web traffic
characteristicExample.description: The lack of encryption enables an external adversary to read the personal data being exchanged with the system.
characteristicExample.fullDescription: If web traffic to a website is not encrypted, external adversaries may be able to read all the personal data exchanged with that website.

impact.name: Excessive data exposure
impact.description: Overexposure of personal data may lead to unintended consequences, as others could reuse the data for unforeseen purposes.

criteria.name: Accessibility
criteria.description: How accessible is the data (public/limited/private)?

additionalInformation.name: Consider parties with whom data is shared
